sources.news_title: Saudi Arabia: Many Dead in Attack on Airport in Riyadh
sources.text:
Saudi-Arabien Viele Tote bei Angriff auf Flughafen in Riad
Etwa 40 Millionen Passagiere nutzen den Flughafen in der saudischen Hauptstadt Riad jedes Jahr. Zuletzt wurde er mehrfach angegriffen. Nun gab es wieder eine Attacke - mindestens zwölf Menschen starben. Diplomaten vermuten die Huthi-Miliz hinter dem Angriff.
Immer wieder war der Flughafen der saudischen Hauptstadt Riad zuletzt Ziel von Angriffen. Nun ist das Gelände des Airports erneut beschossen worden. Zwölf Menschen starben. Laut der Luftfahrtbehörde haben vier der getöteten Menschen die saudische Staatsangehörigkeit und zwei die von Bangladesch. Ums Leben kamen auch jeweils eine Person aus den USA, Ägypten, Jordanien, Syrien sowie aus dem Sudan und den palästinensischen Gebieten.
Die Behörden melden außerdem mindestens 309 Verletzte, einige schweben in Lebensgefahr.
Stecken die Huthi hinter dem Angriff?
Zuletzt hatte die Huthi-Miliz aus dem Jemen den Flughafen in Riad angegriffen. Ob sie auch hinter der neuerlichen Attacke steckt, ist unklar.
Nach Angaben aus Diplomatenkreisen hatte die Miliz am Nachmittag eine Rakete auf den Flughafen abgefeuert. Die saudische Luftfahrtbehörde bestätigte einen Angriff auf den Flughafen, machte aber nicht offiziell die Huthis für die Attacke verantwortlich. Von der Miliz gibt es bisher kein Bekennerschreiben.
Warnung vor Nutzung des Flughafens
Wegen des Angriffs wurde der Betrieb am King-Khalid-Airports vorübergehend eingestellt. Die Bundesregierung rät bis auf Weiteres dringend von der Nutzung des Flughafens ab. Wie das Auswärtige Amt in Berlin mitteilte, muss in Saudi-Arabien mit weiteren Luftangriffen sowie mit Beeinträchtigungen des Flugverkehrs gerechnet werden.
Auch Spanien und Kanada warnten ihre Staatsangehörigen vor einer Nutzung des Flughafens. Die Fluggesellschaft Kuwait Airways gab die Streichung von zwei Flügen von und nach Riad bekannt und verwies zur Begründung auf die Schließung des Flughafens und die dortige "Sicherheitslage".
Greift Trump nun doch ein?
US-Präsident Donald Trump erwägt inzwischen offenbar, Saudi-Arabien im Kampf die Huthis zu unterstützen. Nach dem Angriff auf den Flughafen von Riad werde seine Regierung nun "sehr schnell" eine Entscheidung treffen, Trump vor Journalisten am Weißen Haus. US-Medien zufolge hatten die USA Bitten Saudi-Arabiens um militärische Unterstützung bisher abgelehnt.
Saudi-Arabien kämpft gegen die Huthi im Jemen
Zuletzt hatte die mit dem Iran verbündete Huthi-Miliz im Jemen ihre Angriffe auf das benachbarte Saudi-Arabien verstärkt und sich auch zu Anschlägen mit ballistischen Raketen auf den Flughafen von Riad und andere Einrichtungen bekannt.
Saudi-Arabien führt eine Militärkoalition an, die die international anerkannte Regierung des Jemen im Kampf gegen die Huthi unterstützt. Die Miliz kontrolliert seit Jahren weite Teile des Jemen, darunter die Hauptstadt Sanaa. Zuletzt übernahm sie nach einer Blitzoffensive die Kontrolle über große Teile der Küste an der strategisch und wirtschaftlich wichtigen Meerenge Bab al-Mandab.

sources.news_title: Saudi Arabia: 12 dead, 309 injured in Riyadh airport attack | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Saudi Arabia: 12 dead, 309 injured in Riyadh airport attack
Saudi Arabia said 12 people were killed and 309 were injured today in an attack on the Riyadh airport, the deadliest incident in an intensifying conflict with Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended temporarily while the damage was being assessed. Some of the injured were in critical condition.
The U.S. warned its citizens to avoid the airport in the Saudi capital. One of the people killed was an American, according to Saudi Arabia. The U.K. described the latest incident as “serious” and airlines including Kuwait’s national carrier scrapped flights.
About 260 flights to and from Riyadh were canceled today and another 219 were delayed, according to data from air traffic monitor Flightradar24.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport issued an alert to passengers asking that they contact airlines directly and confirm the status of their flights before heading to the airport.
Three Saudi nationals were killed in an attack on the airport on Thursday and others were injured, while a Saudia Airlines aircraft was damaged, the Saudi authorities said. Earlier attacks this week killed one person at the capital’s main airport and two at Abha airport. Both strikes were claimed by the Iran-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
The Houthis are facing a ground offensive from a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. Soldiers from the internationally recognized Yemeni government and the Saudi air force are working to take back territory won by the militant group over the past month near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The offensive began on Sunday and the coalition says it has gained ground, including retaking the Red Sea port city of Mokha. The Saudi-led group says it aims to “eliminate” the Houthis, who control territory that is home to around 70% of Yemen’s population, including the capital, Sanaa.
President Donald Trump said today that he was being briefed on the Riyadh airport attack. Asked by reporters whether the U.S. would join the Saudi attacks on Houthi rebels, he responded, “We may. We’re going to look at it.”
He added, “We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision.”
Up to now, the Trump administration has been reluctant to get more involved in the Saudi offensive.
This Bloomberg News story was distributed by Tribune News Service.

sources.news_title: Egyptian Woman Among 12 Killed in Riyadh Airport Attack
sources.text:
An Egyptian woman was among 12 people killed in Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said on Sunday.
A medical source at a Riyadh hospital told AFP on Saturday that the Egyptian victim worked as a flight attendant for a Saudi airline. Neither Saudi nor Egyptian authorities have publicly named her.
In a follow-up statement dated 11 October, GACA said those killed were four Saudi citizens and eight residents: two from Bangladesh, and one each from Egypt, the United States, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Another 309 people were injured, some of them critically, and are being treated at several hospitals.
The authority said the attack also caused property damage, which is still being assessed.
GACA did not say who carried out the attack, which hit the airport on Saturday afternoon. A diplomatic source told AFP that a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis struck the airport at around 3pm local time.
The Houthis had not claimed the strike by Saturday night, Reuters reported. After the attack, the group’s military spokesperson reposted an earlier message saying only pre-approved humanitarian flights could land at Riyadh airport, adding the words “a reminder.”
The Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities since Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, launched an offensive last weekend to retake territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saturday’s strike was the third attack on King Khalid International Airport this week. On 6 and 7 October, attacks on Abha International Airport and the Riyadh airport killed three residents, a Moroccan woman and an Algerian woman in Abha and a Sudanese man in Riyadh, according to GACA. Eight people were injured in Riyadh, among them two Egyptian residents.
On Thursday, three Saudi citizens, including a Saudia pilot, were killed in attacks on the airport and a Saudia aircraft, GACA said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the earlier attacks.
Egypt’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned Saturday’s attack in a statement that evening, calling it a flagrant violation of international law and a disregard for “the safety of civilians of various nationalities.”
The ministry said Egypt stands with Saudi Arabia and supports the steps it takes to protect its security and sovereignty. The statement was issued before GACA announced the death toll.
Earlier on Saturday, the ministry had condemned Thursday’s attacks and offered its condolences to the Saudi government and people.
After the earlier attack in which two Egyptians were injured, Egypt’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Hatem Abdel Kader, and the consul general in Riyadh, Yasser Hashem, visited one of them in hospital. The second has since left hospital, Al-Qahera News reported.
Operations at the airport were suspended after the attack, and flight-tracking data showed all flights to Riyadh diverted or cancelled. Qatar Airways, Etihad and Kuwait Airways cancelled flights to the Saudi capital, while the US and Canadian embassies told their citizens to avoid the airport.
Egypt Air suspends services to Riyadh
EgyptAir suspended its flights from Cairo and Alexandria to Riyadh until operations at King Khalid airport resume, in coordination with Saudi civil aviation authorities. Passengers holding confirmed tickets on the cancelled flights can change their route to any other Saudi city EgyptAir flies to directly, with no change fees or fare differences, the airline said. Those who prefer to cancel can get a refund without cancellation fees.
EgyptAir said its operations centre is monitoring the situation around the clock, and asked passengers to check their bookings through its call centre.
Air Cairo also suspended its flights between Riyadh and both Cairo and Sohag on 11 and 12 October, and asked passengers to contact the airline or their travel agent.

sources.news_title: At least 12 people killed, more than 300 injured in strike on Riyadh airport, Saudi officials say
sources.text:
At least 12 people killed, more than 300 injured in strike on Riyadh airport, Saudi officials say
At least 12 people, including one American, were killed and 309 others injured in a strike Saturday on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, according to Saudi officials.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said those killed included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis and one person each from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Those injured were receiving treatment at several hospitals, officials said in a social media post. Several people were in critical condition.
The Saudi kingdom has faced an extraordinary series of assaults on the new front in the Iran war. President Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
"We may. We're gonna look at it," Mr. Trump said earlier Saturday when asked about the possibility. "We just found out about the recent attack [on the airport]. So we'll make a decision — we move very quickly."
A U.S. State Department spokesperson on Saturday condemned "Houthi terrorist attacks against civilian infrastructure and airports." The Iran-backed Houthis have not yet claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike.
The spokesperson told CBS News the State Department is in close contact with its "Saudi partners."
The Houthis, though, claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. In Saturday's strike, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
Riyadh airport operations have been suspended
Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry, hours after the latest one, was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Though the Houthis have told The Associated Press and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged on the ground, with no passengers on board.

sources.news_title: Saudi Authorities Say Attack on Riyadh Airport Killed 12 People and Wounded Over 300 More
sources.text:
CAIRO (AP) — Saudi authorities say an attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more.
The statement says the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
It said some of those injured were in critical condition.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
The international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, was attacked again Saturday as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war.
President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.
On Saturday, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights and many people were wounded, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said of intervening. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
Riyadh airport operations have been suspended
Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended and the extent of injuries and damage was being assessed. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight.
The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist.
The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.”
Flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.”
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes.
The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
___
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Attack on Saudi airport leaves 12 dead, dozens wounded
sources.text:
The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, they said 309 were wounded.
Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.
Saturday’s attack occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia’s threat warning system. This week’s two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.
This week’s deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s self-defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children.
Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had “shut down Riyadh international airport”. The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.
US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.
Riyadh due to hold major summits
Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.
Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.
Organizers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security.

sources.news_title: Saudi Arabia Says 12 Killed, 309 Injured in Attack on Riyadh Airport
sources.text:
Saudi Arabia Says 12 Killed, 309 Injured in Attack on Riyadh Airport
An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309 others, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said early Sunday, as the kingdom faced renewed strikes following an escalation in fighting with Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen.
The assault on October 10 struck the airport’s passenger facilities, prompting authorities to suspend operations, evacuate affected areas, and assess the damage. No group immediately claimed responsibility, although the Houthis had acknowledged previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week.
The aviation authority said four Saudi citizens were among those killed. The other victims included two Bangladeshis and one national each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, the Palestinian territories, and Sudan.
The 309 injured were receiving treatment at hospitals, with some in critical condition, according to the authority. Officials were continuing to evaluate damage to airport infrastructure.

Saturday’s strike was the latest in a series of attacks targeting the airport. On Thursday, two assaults killed three Saudi citizens, including a Saudia airline pilot, and damaged an aircraft belonging to the national carrier. Flights had subsequently resumed before the latest attack forced another suspension.
The renewed violence follows intensified fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and forces aligned with the internationally recognized government, which receives Saudi support.
The Houthis have targeted Saudi airports, military installations, and energy facilities while fighting continues over territory and strategic routes, including approaches to the Bab el Mandeb Strait.

sources.news_title: Houthi attack on Saudi airport kills 12, over 300 wounded, authorities say
Riyadh airport attack kills at least 12, injures more than 300, Saudi authorities say
sources.text:
Riyadh airport attack kills at least 12, injures more than 300, Saudi authorities say
A Riyadh airport attack killed 12 people and injured over 300, as regional tensions escalated.
An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, Saudi authorities said. Some of the injured were in critical condition, according to the statement.
The dead included four Saudi citizens and nationals of Bangladesh, Palestine, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. The attack comes amid escalating strikes on Saudi Arabia as the Iran war widens across the region.
Airport operations suspended
Saudi civil aviation authorities suspended operations at Riyadh airport following the attack and began assessing the damage and injuries. An official aviation notice said the suspension would remain in place until midnight.
Flights were diverted to other airports, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24. Several airlines had already suspended services to Riyadh and other Saudi airports amid growing security concerns.
The attack came days after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for earlier strikes on the airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot, according to the Associated Press. A regional official said a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, on Saturday.
Iran war widens regional tensions
The latest attack comes amid a surge in strikes targeting Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure. The escalation followed a major military offensive by a Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis in Yemen.
US President Donald Trump said he was considering whether Washington should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis. Asked about possible intervention, Trump said the administration would assess the latest attack before making a decision.
The Houthis have also accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport, in Yemen's Houthi-controlled capital. Fighting between the rebels and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has intensified, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support to government forces.
Also Read: Trump weighs joining the fight against Houthis after Saudi capital's airport is struck again
The attacks have also disrupted air travel. FlightAware recorded at least 291 cancellations at Riyadh airport over the preceding 24 hours, while aviation authorities warned of increased risks to civilian aircraft operating in Saudi airspace.
Saudi authorities have also cautioned the public against filming or sharing information about missile and drone interceptions and their impact sites, warning that doing so could carry legal consequences.

sources.news_title: Report: At least 12 killed, 50 wounded in attack on Saudi airport

sources.news_title: 1 American among 12 killed, over 300 injured in airport attack, Saudi authorities say
sources.text:
The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition.
The attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi-backed government forces there.
Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are
The statement, which did not assign blame for the attack, said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.
Create a free account with NBC 5 DFW to save articles and videos.
Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said of intervening. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
U.S. & World
Riyadh airport operations have been suspended
Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended and the extent of injuries and damage was being assessed. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and a Houthi-launched ballistic missile had been intercepted in Al-Kharj governorate, southeast of Riyadh.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
Earlier Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.”
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.”
___
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Suspected Houthi attack on Riyadh airport kills two, wounds dozens: medical sources
sources.text:
At least 12 dead in Riyadh airport attack: Saudi officials
The attack prompted Saudi health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency", a medical source said.
RIYADH: At least 12 people were killed and 309 others wounded Saturday (Oct 10) in a strike on Riyadh's international airport, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation officials said - an attack that a diplomatic source blamed on Yemen's Houthis.
Four Saudi citizens were among the dead, as well as two Bangladeshis, one US citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the statement added. Some of the wounded were in serious condition.
The Iran-backed Houthis have unleashed a wave of strikes against the kingdom at an unprecedented scale, targeting Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers since a truce in their long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, and aviation officials did not mention the Houthis by name.
The diplomatic source attributed the attack to a Houthi missile.
Operations were suspended at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport following the attack, the Saudi civil aviation authority said earlier.
Damages were still being assessed.
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency situation", a medical source said.
Foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
"SERIOUS EMERGENCY SITUATION"
One passenger told AFP they witnessed a strike in the airport's domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
Hours after the Riyadh attack, a spokesman for the Saudi-led international coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said in a post on X that a "projectile" had landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
And then early Sunday, the coalition said it had intercepted a missile southeast of the capital.
The Houthis claimed a series of strikes targeting the airport on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new attacks on Saturday.
Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Mecca had been among the wounded.
US "MAY" JOIN SAUDI STRIKES
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour's conflict.
US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for American military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, US President Donald Trump said: "We may."
"We're going to look at it," he told reporters in front of the White House. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision."
The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia called on their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies had said they were banning their staff from using the airport "over the next week".
Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station.
The latest attack comes on the eve of Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
"MOVING UP THE ESCALATION LADDER"
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area - a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping - but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.
Analyst Anna Jacob of the Arab Gulf States Institute predicted the Saudis would take an even tougher tack against the Houthis in response to the recent attacks.
"One thing is for sure, we are moving up the escalation ladder in a very dangerous way," she said.
"The Yemeni government and the Saudis have gone in hard in Yemen to reverse Houthi gains, and the Houthis are responding with significant escalation."

sources.news_title: Attack on Saudi airport leaves 12 dead, dozens wounded, sources say
sources.text:
Houthi attack on Saudi airport kills 12, over 300 wounded, authorities say
By Timour Azhari and Enas Alashray
RIYADH, Oct 10 (Reuters) - The third attack this week on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left at least 12 people dead and more than 300 wounded, Saudi authorities said, as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.
The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, officials said, 309 were wounded.
Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.
Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. This week's two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.
The deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.
A Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond to the attack.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport". The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.
US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.
EYEWITNESS SAW WOUNDED ON THE GROUND
One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.
An injuredtraveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.
The US embassy in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."
Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.
The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.
That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.
RIYADH DUE TO HOLD MAJOR SUMMITS
Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.
Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.
Organizers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.
(Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh; Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington DC; Writing by Enas Alashray and Maya Gebeily, Ann Saphir;Editing by Gareth Jones, Joe Bavier and David Gregorio)

sources.news_title: Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
sources.text:
Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.
"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.
Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.
At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."
Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
What do we know about the Riyadh attack?
A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.
The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."
Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."
What did the Houthis say?
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.
However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.
In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."
When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."
Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week
Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.
Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.
Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.
The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.
The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

sources.news_title: 12 killed, 309 injured in attack on Riyadh airport as Houthis, Saudi Arabia trade strikes
sources.text:
RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- An attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday afternoon has killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said, as Yemen's Houthi group and Saudi Arabia continued exchanging strikes on major airports.
The Saudi aviation authority said in a statement early Sunday that the fatalities included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign residents -- two Bangladeshis and one each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan.
The injured are receiving treatment at several hospitals, with some in serious condition, the authority said.
The authority said in an earlier statement that operations at the airport had been temporarily suspended pending damage assessments and safety checks.
Following the Saturday attack, the Houthi group said in a statement that it was ready for reciprocal measures with Saudi Arabia to keep airports, seaports and other facilities with humanitarian functions outside the escalating military confrontation.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported Saturday that Saudi Arabia launched a new wave of air and missile strikes across Houthi-held areas in Yemen, targeting Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held capital, areas near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait and several northern provinces.
Also on Saturday, Yemen's government forces said that more than 1,150 Houthi fighters had been "neutralized" and over 180 military and logistical vehicles destroyed or damaged in over 1,900 strikes across multiple fronts in Yemen in the past 24 hours.
The figures could not be independently verified.
Around Yemen's southwestern city of Taiz, Houthi advances have put increasing pressure on government forces defending the city and disrupted key roads connecting it with government-held areas in southern Yemen, government military sources told Xinhua, adding that fierce clashes were underway south of the city.
Supported by Saudi airstrikes, the Yemeni government launched a large-scale offensive on Monday, seeking to retake Houthi-held territory, with some of the fiercest fighting concentrated around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, now based in the southern port city of Aden. The renewed fighting marked a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

sources.news_title: Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, 309 injured in Yemeni strike on Riyadh’s airport
12 killed, 309 injured in devastating attack on Saudi Arabia’s busiest airport
sources.text:
At least 12 people have been killed and 309 injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority has announced.
The authority said some of the injured remained in critical condition following Saturday’s attack on the kingdom’s busiest airport.
Those killed were four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals and one person each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. No Zimbabwean was listed among the fatalities announced by authorities.
Airport operations were temporarily suspended while emergency teams responded and officials assessed the damage. Flights were cancelled or diverted from Riyadh following the strike.
The attack was the third to hit the airport within a week amid an escalating conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for two earlier attacks on the airport, which killed several people and damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft. However, there was no immediate claim of responsibility for Saturday’s deadly strike.
A projectile was also reported to have landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen.
Several foreign governments advised their citizens to avoid King Khalid International Airport and surrounding areas as authorities dealt with the aftermath.
United States President Donald Trump said Washington was assessing whether it would participate in Saudi military action against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump told reporters after being asked about a possible American response.
The attack represents a major escalation in the renewed regional confrontation and has raised fresh concerns about the safety of civilian aviation in Saudi airspace.
King Khalid International Airport serves Riyadh and is one of the Middle East’s most important aviation hubs.

sources.news_title: At least 12 dead, over 300 hurt in attack on Riyadh airport
sources.text:
LAJHORE AIRPORT (AFP) — An attack on Riyadh’s international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded 309 others, some of them seriously, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation officials said on Saturday.
Four Saudi citizens were among the dead, as well as two Bangladeshis, one US citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the statement added.
Saudi authorities suspended operations at Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday after a fresh attack there left multiple people wounded.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the “serious emergency”, a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility.
Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday.
Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said 155 arriving and 161 departing flights had been cancelled, while a total of 222 flights were delayed.
AP and Reuters, amongst others, reporting a strike on Riyadh Airport this afternoon. Last commercial aircraft to land was 14:05 Local time. The last departure was at 13:39 LT. Flights bound for RUH are diverting elsewhere, mainly to Jeddah at the moment. https://t.co/qdT3aOyLdf https://t.co/HiuRaOoLPS
— Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 10, 2026
At around 6pm local time, Flightradar24 noted that flights bound for the airport were “diverting elsewhere, mainly to Jeddah at the moment”. It later shared a notice to airmen (Notam) for operations suspended till 12am.
A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic.
“I was on gate 403” at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP. “I saw 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday.
“We were told we are dealing with a ‘serious emergency situation’. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh”, with many in critical condition, the source said.
The aviation authority said the number of injured from the attack was still being assessed, adding that airport “operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities”.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July.
A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with “dozens of people injured” in all.
A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass. Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.
Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Makkah had been injured while waiting to board their flight.
A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by “a missile around 3:00pm” (5pm PKT).
“Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target,” the source said.

sources.news_title: 12 People Killed in Houthi Rebel Missile Attack On Riyadh King Khalid International Airport, 300 Injured
sources.text:
Saudi officials confirmed late on Saturday night that 12 civilians were killed in a Houthi rebel ballistic missile attack on Riyadh King Khalid International Airport (RUH). 309 people were also wounded in the Saturday blast inside the airport’s main Terminal 3 building. Some of the wounded have been critically injured and the death toll could rise in the coming hours.
Amongst the dead is an American citizen, as well as nationals of Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan, Palestine (as recognized by Saudia Arabia), Syria, and Sudan.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed the casualty figure around an hour after several media outlets reported the same number as provided by anonymous intelligence sources.
The GCAA added that the blast resulted in “material damage,” which is still being assessed. All operations have been suspended at King Khalid International Airport, and flights have been grounded.
The attack occurred on Saturday afternoon, as the airport was full of passengers waiting to board planes. The calm of the terminal building was shattered as a massive blast ripped through the concourse. Graphic video of blood-stained hallways has since emerged on social media.
The Houthis first warned airlines and the Saudi Arabian government on October 5 that they would target civil aviation, claiming that airspace and airports aceoss the Kingdom would not be safe.
The rebel group stepped up attacks this week, with King Khalid Airport repeatedly suspending operations temporarily as missile attacks threatened the safety of the facility. Several missiles had already penetrated Saudi Arabia’s missile defense systems, killing civilians and damaging buildings.
On October 6 and October 7, Houthi missiles struck Abha International Airport in the southwest of the Kingdom, killing two people and injuring dozens more. A separate missile attack at King Khalid Airport killed one and injured eight people.
Then, on October 8, King Khalid Airport was targeted in two attacks. The first attack caused damage to a building, while the second attack struck a parked Saudia Airlines Airbus A320 series aircraft which was stationary at the terminal gate.
Three people were killed in this attack, including a Captain for Saudia Airlines.
While local airlines had still been operating flights to and from King Khalid Airport, many international carriers had already suspended their operations to Riyadh in recent days.
Even Saudi Arabia’s regional allies, including the likes of Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Flydubai, have suspended flights due to security concerns.
According to flight tracking service Flight Radar 24, the last commercial aircraft to land at King Khalid Airport on October 10 was at 2:05 pm local time. The last departure was at 1:39 pm.
The Houthis are an armed movement from northern Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s southern neighbour. In 2014, they seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and pushed out the government. In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition into Yemen to restore that government, and the two sides have been enemies ever since.
The group is backed by Iran, which supplies them with missiles and drones. A truce in 2022 brought several quiet years, but it broke down this summer, and Saudi-backed forces are now fighting to retake Sanaa. The attacks on Saudi airports are the Houthi response.
A slew of international governments, including the US, UK, France, and Canada, have urged their citizens to avoid King Khalid Airport. On Saturday, the US State Department updated its travel advice for Saudi Arabia for the first time since mid-September, saying there remained a “risk of drone and missile targeting of American interests by Iran and the Iranian-supported Houthis.”

sources.news_title: Attack on Riyadh airport kills 12, wounds more than 300
sources.text:
Attack on Riyadh airport kills 12, wounds more than 300
Samy Magdy and Cara Anna |
Twelve people have been killed in a missile attack on the main airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday injured 309 others, the Saudi civil aviation authority said said in a statement on X.
Some of the injured were in a critical condition, it added.
Airport operations were suspended while authorities evaluated the damage and conducted safety inspections.
This was latest in a string of attacks targeting the oil-rich kingdom’s aviation facilities as it faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militia has stepped up missile and drone attacks on neighbouring Saudi Arabia the past several weeks and has previously claimed responsibility for hits on Riyadh airport and other facilities in the kingdom.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for Saturday’s attack.
The international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh has been attacked again as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war.
US President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.
On Saturday, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights and many people were wounded, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said of intervening.
“We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier on Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The airport in Ryiadh has a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A US bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said US assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region.
Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability”.
The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theatre for their military operations.
At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been cancelled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
